html:
"Saami" is the map's label, from 1500 BCE to 700 CE, for the ancestors of the Sámi, the native people of the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula. The later map label Sámi carries their story through the Middle Ages.

People had lived in the far north since the ice retreated more than 10,000 years ago, hunting reindeer and seals and fishing. The rock carvings at Alta in northern Norway, made over thousands of years, show their world: reindeer, elk, boats and fishing. The Sámi languages belong to the Uralic family, like Finnish. Linguists think the early Sámi language spread into the north during the first millennium BCE, through contact with the forest peoples to the east, and was taken up by people already living there.

Through these centuries they lived by hunting wild reindeer, often driving herds into pits and fences, by fishing and sealing on the coast, and by gathering. Families moved between seasonal camps. Metal came to them through trade with the south and east.

Writers far to the south noticed them. In 98 CE Tacitus described the "Fenni", hunters with no horses or houses who tipped their arrows with bone; many scholars think he meant the Sámi. In the 500s Procopius and Jordanes wrote of the "Skrithiphinoi" or "Screrefennae", the skiing Finns. Their southern neighbours were Germanic farmers, among them the Swedes.
